result: Drosophila perform a body location-prioritized grooming sequence when mechanosensory neurons are simultaneously stimulated by dust, consistent with a parallel model where eye grooming occurs first because it suppresses grooming of other locations.
evaluation: Claims C1, C8, C9, and C10 are all supported by citations to previous work (Hampel et al., 2017; Seeds et al., 2014; Mueller et al., 2019; Phillis et al., 1993) establishing the dust-induced grooming sequence and its consistency with the parallel model. These claims provide the foundational behavioral context for the current study.

result: Nearly all mechanosensory neurons on the Drosophila head that elicit aimed grooming were identified and their projections reconstructed, providing the first synaptic resolution somatotopic map of a head with neighboring BMNs projecting to overlapping zones and showing higher connectivity similarity than distant BMNs.
evaluation: Claims C2-C4, C19-C21 are supported by comprehensive experimental data including optogenetic activation (C19), anatomical reconstructions using multiple methods (C3), and connectomic analysis (C21). The combination of light microscopy, dye fills, transgenic driver lines, and EM reconstructions provides converging evidence for the somatotopic organization.

result: Head bristles were classified and quantified, and BMNs innervating bristles at different head locations were found to project through specific nerves including the antennal, eye, occipital, and labial nerves.
evaluation: Claims C22-C36 are supported by imaging data (C22), transgenic expression patterns (C23), and anatomical reconstruction data (C24-C36). The identification of the previously undescribed occipital nerve (C27) and comprehensive mapping of BMN projections through different nerves provides essential anatomical foundation for the somatotopic map.

result: All head BMN nerves project into the subesophageal zone (SEZ) of the ventral brain, with BMNs from different nerves projecting into distinct zones, though some potential overlap exists.
evaluation: Claims C37-C41 are supported by anatomical observations using transgenic driver lines and computational alignment of expression patterns (C40). The identification of all head BMN projections terminating in the SEZ (C38) is well-documented through multiple driver lines and imaging approaches.

result: Optogenetic activation of different BMN types elicits aimed grooming of specific head locations and neighboring locations, with dorsal head BMNs eliciting dorsal head grooming, BM-Taste neurons eliciting labellar and neighboring grooming, and posterior head BMNs eliciting head nodding in two behavioral contexts.
evaluation: Claims C42-C49 are supported by optogenetic behavioral experiments with multiple driver lines (dBMN-spGAL4, TasteBMN-spGAL4, InOmBMN-LexA, pBMN-spGAL4) and video documentation. The inference that BMNs elicit grooming of both corresponding and neighboring locations (C46) is well-supported by the experimental data, though the exact resolution of the parallel architecture remains to be fully determined.

result: Somatotopically organized head BMNs elicit both aimed grooming and avoidance-like responses including backward motions and head nodding, with these movements being mutually exclusive and sequential.
evaluation: Claims C50-C52 and C126-C132 are supported by optogenetic behavioral observations showing backward motions with dorsal head and eye BMN activation (C50, C128, C129) and head nodding with posterior head BMN activation (C130). The citation to previous work on avoidance responses (C131) and synthesis of current experimental data (C132) provide converging evidence.

result: This work provides the most comprehensive definition of BMNs for any body part of Drosophila, though some knowledge gaps remain regarding PoOc and Su bristles.
evaluation: Claims C53-C54 are supported by the comprehensive reconstruction effort validated against bristle counts. The acknowledgment of knowledge gaps (C55) and speculative proposals about unidentified neurons (C56-C57) appropriately qualify the completeness of the work while maintaining that nearly all head BMNs were reconstructed.

result: The neurotransmitter identity of head BMNs remains unresolved, though machine learning predictions suggest they are overwhelmingly cholinergic.
evaluation: Claim C58 is based on unpublished machine learning predictions and a single citation to previous work on leg BMNs (Tuthill and Wilson, 2016a). Claim C59 acknowledges conflicting evidence from different studies. The lack of direct experimental validation of neurotransmitter identity in head BMNs makes this result uncertain.

result: The reconstruction and annotation of head mechanosensory neurons (JONs, BMNs, TPMNs) in FAFB reveals modality-specific projections with BMNs showing somatotopic organization and JONs showing tonotopic organization, with potential overlap between JO-F neurons and some BMNs.
evaluation: Claims C60-C65 are supported by anatomical reconstruction data (C61) and citations to previous work on JON organization (C62). The observation of potential overlap between JO-F neurons and BMNs (C63) and the inference that JO-F projections may be somatotopic (C64) are appropriately qualified as preliminary observations requiring further investigation.

result: This work defines the somatotopic organization of head BMNs using EM reconstructions to produce a comprehensive synaptic resolution map, showing that all reconstructed head BMN types terminate in the SEZ where the first layers of BMN processing occur.
evaluation: Claims C66-C72 are supported by comprehensive EM reconstruction data and appropriate contextualization with previous work (C67-C69). The observation that all head BMN types terminate in the SEZ (C71) contrasts with other insects where head BMNs project to both SEZ and thoracic ganglia (C73), highlighting a potentially Drosophila-specific feature.

result: Head BMNs of the same type show stereotyped morphology, project to the same SEZ zones, and show the highest postsynaptic connectivity similarity, though some BMN types show intratype diversity with subtypes having differing morphology and connectivity.
evaluation: Claims C74-C77 are supported by anatomical reconstruction data from multiple individuals (C74), citations to previous work across multiple species (C75), and connectomic analysis (C76-C77). The identification of BMN subtypes (C77) and the example of BM-InOm neuron diversity (C78) are well-supported by NBLAST and cosine similarity clustering data.

result: BMN types innervating neighboring bristle populations have overlapping projections into zones corresponding to dorsal, ventral, and posterior head regions, with neighboring BMNs showing common postsynaptic partners, though overlap is only partial.
evaluation: Claims C79-C82 are supported by anatomical reconstruction data (C79), connectomic analysis (C80-C81), and appropriate inference about functional significance (C82). Citations to previous work showing similar overlap in other body parts (C83-C85) provide comparative context. The speculation about functional implications for grooming (C86) is appropriately qualified.

result: Some head BMNs have ipsilateral-only projections while others have midline-crossing projections, with BMNs innervating medially located bristles on the anterior head showing midline-crossing projections similar to patterns observed in other body parts and insect species, though the organizational logic may not be universal.
evaluation: Claims C87-C88 are supported by EM reconstruction data. Claims C89-C91 provide comparative context through citations to previous work in Drosophila and other insects. The speculation about functional implications (C92) and acknowledgment that the organizational logic may not be universal (C93-C94) are appropriately qualified based on observations of exceptions.

result: This work provides the first synaptic resolution somatotopic map of a head for any species, overcoming previous limitations of sparse labeling and extrapolation across animals, with important implications for understanding somatotopic neural circuit organization.
evaluation: Claims C95 and C100 are supported by the comprehensive EM reconstruction methods and data presented. Claims C96-C99 appropriately contextualize the novelty by citing previous work and assessing limitations of previous studies. Claims C101-C102 about future implications are reasonable inferences from the comprehensive dataset provided.

result: Activation of head BMNs elicits aimed grooming of specific head locations, with BM-InOm neurons eliciting eye grooming and other BMN types eliciting grooming of dorsal and ventral head, extending previous findings that BMNs are important for eliciting aimed grooming across the head and body.
evaluation: Claims C103 and C108 are supported by optogenetic behavioral experiments. Claims C104-C107 and C109 provide appropriate context through citations to previous behavioral studies. Claim C110 represents a well-supported synthesis. Claims C111-C112 are supported by optogenetic data, while C113 is appropriately labeled as a hypothesis. Claim C114 cites previous validation of the optogenetic approach.

result: Different evidence supports the hypothesis that BMNs connect with parallel circuits that each elicit a different aimed grooming movement, including cosine similarity analysis revealing parallel connectivity with partial convergence of neighboring BMN types, and identification of a connected antennal grooming circuit.
evaluation: Claims C115-C117 are supported by connectomic analysis data. Claims C118-C121 are supported by citations to previous work identifying circuits and their components. Claim C122 about preliminary connectomic analysis is appropriately qualified as unpublished data. The convergence of multiple lines of evidence supports the parallel circuit hypothesis, though the exact resolution remains to be fully determined.

result: Activation of specific BMN types elicits aimed grooming of both their corresponding bristle locations and neighboring locations, providing a means of cleaning the area surrounding the stimulus location, with the hypothesis that neighboring BMNs connect with common neural circuits.
evaluation: Claim C123 is supported by optogenetic behavioral experiments. Claim C124 represents a reasonable inference from the behavioral observations. Claim C125 is appropriately labeled as a hypothesis integrating anatomical, connectomic, and behavioral data, though it requires further experimental validation.

result: This study defines the parallel architecture of BMN types that elicit the head grooming sequence, with distinct projections and connectivity among BMNs innervating distant bristles supporting the parallel architecture, though partially overlapping projections among neighboring BMNs raise questions about the resolution of the parallel architecture.
evaluation: Claims C133-C138 are supported by citations to previous work establishing the parallel model framework and optogenetic evidence. Claims C139 and C141 are supported by the comprehensive anatomical and connectomic data presented. Claim C142 appropriately identifies an important unresolved question about the resolution of the parallel architecture based on the observation of partial overlap among neighboring BMNs.

result: The parallel-projecting head BMNs are hypothesized to connect with postsynaptic circuits that perform additional functions to produce the grooming sequence through hierarchical suppression and dust detection, though the presumed role of BMNs in detecting dust remains to be directly demonstrated.
evaluation: Claims C143-C152 are based on the parallel model framework from previous work and represent hypotheses about circuit function that have not been directly tested in the current study. Claims C153-C156 appropriately acknowledge that the role of BMNs in dust detection has not been directly demonstrated, with C154 citing negative results and C155 offering speculation about compensation. This represents an important area for future work.

result: 705 BMNs were identified and reconstructed from EM data, revealing somatotopic organization with three key features: each BMN type has unique branch morphology defining distinct SEZ zones, neighboring BMN types have partially overlapping projections, and projections either remain ipsilateral or cross the midline depending on bristle location.
evaluation: Claims C157-C165 are all supported by EM reconstruction data and the matching process between EM and light microscopy data. The three features of somatotopic organization (C160-C164) are well-documented through comprehensive anatomical analysis. Claim C165 represents an appropriate synthesis of the EM reconstruction data.
